content.text:
The four-die cancellation comes from the incoming source record, not from any stored piece. Its text reads: "The more powerful version of the upcoming Rubin Ultra chip with four compute dies has also been canceled. Only the smaller two-die version remains, delivering roughly half the real-world compute performance." The same claim appears as item:e5 and item:e6 in the other_source_records list. Both are attributed to SemiAnalysis, relayed by The Decoder on 2026-07-06. None of the stored pieces (e64 through e102) says this. So I had no stored id to cite for it, and my argument should have said so. I wrote "the new report adds" without giving any id for that point, which left it uncited.

The support_ids I chose for v11 and v13 were e64, e66, e98, e100, e101, e70, e71 and e99. I did not take them from a single governing instruction. The procedure governs how a record is classified: same_claim_as, revises, opposes, or otherwise. The support_ids field in the output schema asks for the piece ids the argument rests on. I selected pieces that carry the Kyber delay claim, which the incoming record repeats, and I classified them as same_claim_as. I added e70 and e71 because they carry the same SemiAnalysis delay and PCB-midplane claim, though they were not in v11's existing piece_ids. I placed e65, e72 and e102 in opposing_ids because they are Nvidia's denials of the delay. I included e99 because it states that Kyber houses 144 Rubin Ultra GPUs and was originally slated for 2027, which gives the baseline the delay is measured against.

Two citation choices I considered and rejected:

1. Citing item:e8 as support for the claim that Nvidia will make up the shortfall with more Oberon-Rubin racks. That sentence is The Decoder's own writing, not SemiAnalysis's, so it is not a SemiAnalysis claim. I left it out of the argument's evidence and mentioned it only in new_information with that attribution.

2. Treating e101 as independent support for the NVL72x2 scrapping. e101 is the same SemiAnalysis report relayed by datacenterdynamics. I classified it as same_claim_as and set independent_sources to false, so it adds no second source.

Stated in the texts, as opposed to my inference:

- Stated: SemiAnalysis reports the four-die Rubin Ultra was canceled, that only the two-die version remains at roughly half the real-world compute, and that CPO-NVSwitch will not arrive until Feynman. These are SemiAnalysis rumour via The Decoder, and Nvidia's only response is "Our roadmap is intact."
- Stated: Kyber cabinets house 144 Rubin Ultra GPUs and were originally slated for 2027 (e99). The delay to 2028 is stated as a SemiAnalysis claim (e64, e66, e98).
- Inference: that the four-die cancellation applies to the Kyber NVL144 configuration. The texts never state this mapping, and I should have flagged it as an unstated link rather than treating it as a Kyber condition change. I did note the limitation in the v11 and v13 arguments, but the lean I gave still leaned on it.
- Inference: that the four-die cancellation and the CPO-NVSwitch deferral push the odds of a 2027 or 2028 Kyber launch down. That is my judgement, not a reported fact.
- Inference: that the 2028 delay leaves a Yes lean for v13. This rests on the delay claim being roughly accurate. The denial and the unresolved manufacturing issue make it weak, and I should have said so more clearly.
